title: Drill a straight 1/4 in hole through a 2x4 with a handheld drill, in at the top mark and out at the bottom mark
instruction: Drill a hole straight down through the board, in at the X on its top edge and out at the X on its bottom edge, then put the drill down on the bench and let go of it.
context: Boring a straight hole through lumber with a handheld drill, at a bench or on sawhorses before the piece goes in, is routine carpentry. O*NET lists Core tasks 'Bore boltholes in timber, masonry or concrete walls, using power drill' (Carpenters, 47-2031) and 'Drill holes in timbers or lumber' (Helpers-Carpenters, 47-3012); BLS OEWS May 2025 employment: 670,090 + 21,680 = 691,770. A bolt or rod must come out on its mark on the far face. A shallow hole hides a lean of a few degrees; a through-bore turns it into a miss on the far face: 2.6 degrees off misses the bottom mark of a 3-1/2 in member by 4 mm. So the skill is holding the line under a sustained push until breakthrough, with precise control of position and force on a handheld power tool: set the point on the mark, square the bit while pushing, feed against the reaction twist, and come out on the far mark.
setup: Millimetres; x away from the robot, y to its left, z up from the bench. An SPF 2x4 (38.1 x 88.9 x 300, kiln-dried, about 0.48 kg) stands on edge along y, its centre line at x 330, raised on two 2x4 offcuts laid flat (89 wide, 90 long, 38.1 tall, fixed to the bench with double-sided carpet tape, not screws) centred at x 330 and y -118 and +12, 40 apart under its middle, and held by two 12 in bar clamps along x across its faces, one over each offcut, jaws resting on the offcut at x 300 and 360, each with its fixed jaw on the robot's side and its bar and handle running away from the robot. The sim models only the jaws, as four fixed steel blocks (22 x 40 x 50); the clamps' bars and handles are not simulated, so check on the real bench that they clear the drill's path and the place it is laid down. A 3 mm hardboard scrap on the bench in the gap takes a breakthrough lunge and catches the chips that fall through (not simulated). Pencil Xs (22 mm strokes) mark the middle of the board's top edge and of its bottom edge, at y -53. A 12 V pistol drill/driver (Bosch PS21-2A kit: PS21N pocket driver with a 2.0 Ah battery, or any 12 V pocket drill/driver with a 1/4 in hex holder: 150 x 64 x 178, 846 g with its battery and bit; variable-speed trigger on the front of its rubber-gripped handle; set to forward, high speed (0-1,300 rpm) and a low clutch setting, for example 5 of 20, so a bound bit slips: check it still drills a test hole) lies on its side to the right of the board, bit toward the robot, its handle's centre at (364, -312). The pinch on its handle presses the drill's own trigger (no adapter and no enlarged stand-in); in the demo the pads touch only the rubber handle and the motor housing, 19 mm from the turning holder and over 100 mm from the bit. In it is a 1/4 x 6 in spade bit with a centre point, two cutting spurs and a 1/4 in grooved hex shank (Irwin Speedbor 88804), about 127 exposed; the sim draws it as a plain 1/4 in rod with a pointed tip. For scoring, two phones on tripods film the trial: one at the bench's end looking along the board, one across the bench facing the robot.
scoring: The hole sets the score. Entry: the hole's centre on the top edge, from the top X's centre. Exit: the hole's centre on the bottom edge, from the bottom X's centre. Through: the bit's point got 4 mm past the bottom edge. 1.0: through, entry within 3 mm, exit within 4 mm, the finish, and everything still (under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s) for 1 s. 0.75: through, entry within 3 mm, exit within 8 mm. 0.5: through, entry within 6 mm, exit within 12 mm. 0.25: a hole at least 20 mm deep, entry within 6 mm. The finish, checked at the end: the drill resting on the bench (its lowest point within 5 mm of it; and, seen from above, the rectangle that bounds the drill and its bit, with its sides parallel to the bench's edges, clear of the strip x 286 to 374, y -203 to 97 that holds the board and its offcuts), its trigger released, and every finger at least 50 mm from the drill. Without the finish (the drill still in a hand, left in the hole or lying on the board) the hole scores one step lower: 0.5, 0.25 and 0 in place of 0.75, 0.5 and 0.25 (1.0 needs the finish, so the best hole scores 0.5 without it). 0: anything else. 0 for the whole trial if at any time the drill was dropped (falling faster than 1 m/s, the speed a free fall reaches in 51 mm, with no gripper closed on any part of it; read 20 times a second, so every free fall of 115 mm or more is caught), the bit was levered in its hole (more than 6 degrees between the bit and the line its hole started on, 3 mm in: the hole is reamed oval and its exit thrown off line, and deeper in the side load binds the 1/4 in bit and can bend or snap it), or the drill left the bench top (its centre past an edge of the bench, or any part of it more than 50 mm below the bench top: fallen or carried off it). Running the bit away from the wood, as when starting it or drawing it back out, costs nothing. One hole per trial: once the bit has been drawn fully out of a hole 3 mm deep or more, that hole is the trial's (a second hole or a re-entry adds nothing: the model can't take the bit back into a hole, so a bit drawn fully out before breakthrough leaves a hole that is not through; backing off with the point still in the hole costs nothing; a start lifted off before 3 mm may be moved). Real trial: push a 1/4 in rod into the hole; a ruler from each X's centre to the rod gives entry and exit (turn the board over for the exit), the rod passing shows it is through, and the rod's depth by ruler gives the 20 mm. The trial video shows the set-down, a drop (the drill falling more than about 50 mm with no gripper closed on it), the drill leaving the bench, and whether the bit was drawn fully out before it broke through (the hole then counts as not through, its depth read from the length of bit showing above the board). Levering: in each of the two tripod videos (from the bench's end, and from across the bench), read the drill's lean from the board's top edge with a protractor on a paused frame, once just after the bit has entered and once at its greatest lean while the bit is in the wood; a change of more than 6 degrees in either view is levered (if it changes in both, combine the two as the root of the sum of their squares).
reset_notes: Unclamp the board, slide it along so clear, knot-free wood sits over the gap (holes at least 30 mm apart; a new board when it runs out), mark a fresh pair of Xs at the same place (x 330, y -53, top and bottom edges; carry the lines round with a combination square so the bottom X is exactly under the top one) and clamp it again with the offcuts and clamps at their marked places; fit a fresh bit if the last one is bent or dull; vacuum the chips off the bench and the hardboard scrap (dry, about 3 cm3 a hole, no liquid or sparks; they stay on the board, the bench and the hardboard), and vacuum and wipe the gripper pads (replace a worn pad); lay the drill on its side at its start mark, bit toward the robot, battery charged, set to forward, high speed and the low clutch setting, trigger released. Wood: a kiln-dried SPF 2x4 stud cut into 300 mm pieces, about 3 trials a piece (holes 30 mm apart with the board still fully on both offcuts). A reset takes about 3-4 minutes (an estimate, not timed). An operator stands at the robot's power cut-off whenever the bit can turn.
fidelity: Rigid PhysX bodies at real size and mass. PhysX can't cut wood, so the cut is a feed law: the bit's point (a sprung ball reading the push) advances 0.14 mm/s per N above a 20 N bite, against 0.05 + 0.18 N m per mm/rev (scaled from a spur bit's measured thrust; bite, feed and the 27 N trigger are estimates a bench test would replace). Pushed square it pins; over 8 degrees it skates; from 3 mm in, springs hold the hole's line, binding past 2 degrees. Not simulated: chips, clamp bars, hardboard.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right gripper went to the drill and stayed; the drill is not seen lifted; all 6,000 steps); demo: 1.0 on 3 of 3 trials (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000; success held from about step 3,226). Rule checks: bit run in the air first 1.0; drill left in the hole 0.5; drill dropped 0.
